disease_info: Anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder characterized by persistent restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, and disturbance in the way one’s body weight or shape is experienced or an undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation. Individuals often deny the seriousness of their low body weight and may exhibit rigid, perfectionistic thinking around food, exercise, and achievement. Onset is most common in adolescence and young adulthood, but it can occur or recur later in life, often in the context of stress, loss, or identity shifts. The course can be chronic and relapsing, and it is distinguished from other eating disorders by the marked underweight status and the primary focus on restriction rather than recurrent binge eating or compensatory behaviors alone.

narrative.personality: Marla is a warm, sociable arts enthusiast who pours herself into creative community projects and aesthetic details while quietly holding herself to very high standards.
narrative.stressor: Marla’s difficulties began in her final year of her associate’s program, when a planned transition into a full-time arts administration role fell through and she found herself back at home, juggling part‑time gallery work with unpaid community projects and no clear career path. Feeling behind her peers and increasingly anxious about not “looking the part” of the polished arts professional she followed on Instagram, she started tightening control over what she ate alongside meticulously curating her online presence, telling herself she was just being disciplined and “on brand.” Over time, as internships didn’t materialize and she remained without a stable job, the sense that her body was the one thing she could perfect intensified, and her routines around food and exercise became more rigid and isolating, even as she kept up a cheerful front at events. She finally came to psychiatric attention after family and colleagues repeatedly commented on her marked weight loss and fatigue, and a primary care visit for feeling faint at a gallery opening led to referral when she minimized their concern but could not explain the changes in her eating and weight.
narrative.chief_complaint: My family keeps telling me I’ve gotten way too thin, but I don’t really see it; they’re the ones pushing me to get checked out.

narrative.personality: Ansley is a gentle, methodical homemaker who finds comfort in orderly routines, nurturing others, and quiet, detail‑oriented creative work.
narrative.stressor: Ansley’s problems started after she was told at a routine checkup that her blood pressure and cholesterol were creeping up, and she was advised to lose a bit of weight and exercise more to protect her heart. Already somewhat anxious about aging and determined not to become a “burden,” she threw herself into meal planning and portion control with the same meticulousness she applied to quilting patterns and genealogy charts. As friends at the senior center praised her for looking “so tiny” and she saw the numbers on the scale fall, controlling her food intake became a central way she felt in charge of her body and health, even as her portions grew smaller and mealtimes became increasingly rule‑bound. She agreed to see a psychiatrist only after her primary care physician, worried by her continued weight loss and frailty despite improved labs, urged an evaluation when she insisted she was simply being careful and could not understand why everyone was so worried about how little she was eating.
narrative.chief_complaint: My doctor says I’ve lost too much weight and wants me to talk to someone about it, even though I feel like I’m just being careful with what I eat.

narrative.personality: Sonia is an energetic, curiosity‑driven lecturer who mixes improv-style spontaneity with periods of intense self-criticism and a tendency to overextend herself academically and socially.
narrative.stressor: Sonia’s issues emerged during a period when she was simultaneously taking on a heavier teaching load, starting a master’s program, and applying for a competitive grant, all while many of her close friends were settling into long‑term relationships and family life. Feeling pressure to prove herself professionally and to look “put together” in front of students and colleagues, she began to tighten up her eating and exercise habits as a way to compensate for feeling disorganized and behind in other areas, framing it as a healthy reset. Over months, as work and study demands escalated, she increasingly equated being smaller and more controlled around food with being more disciplined and successful overall, brushing off comments about her weight as jealousy or overreaction. She finally agreed to a psychiatric consultation after a colleague and her program advisor expressed concern that her visible weight loss and preoccupation with maintaining it were affecting her stamina in the classroom and her ability to participate in department events, while she herself continued to insist her weight was fine and not a serious issue.
narrative.chief_complaint: My colleagues keep saying I look too thin and are worried, but I honestly don’t feel like my weight is a serious problem.
